To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the state‐dependent alterations in thermoregressive, cardiovascular, and ventilatory physiology are mediated by central monoamine‐ containing neurons; 2) the monoamines are not the sole mediators of the state‐ dependent physiology, but are the final common pathway for the expression of the state‐specific physiology; 3) the monoamine‐ containing cells are not simply a relay station for the state‐dependent physiology, but are also involved in the generation of the state‐ specific physiological
the thermoregulatory, respiratory, and cardiovascular systems of the rat are state dependent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the state‐dependent aspects of physiological regulation.
the mechanisms by which the brain generates and controls sleep and wakefulness, and how sleep‐wake state changes affect the regulation of thermoregulatory, respiratory, and cardiovascular function.
the state‐dependent alterations in regulatory physiology that are observed when the central nervous system changes from one behavioral state to another.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the state of the animal is a major determinant of the physiological response to a given environmental challenge.
the state‐dependent alterations in physiological function are a consequence of changes in the activity of central monoaminergic neurons.
the sleep‐wake state is an independent variable that has a significant influence on the physiology of the organism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the brain is an important organ of the cardiovascular system.
we have shown how the brain controls breathing, and how the brain can be used to control breathing.
we have shown that the state of sleep and wake can be an important variable that must be considered when studying regulatory physiology.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the state‐dependent physiology that we study in animals is not merely descriptive; it is essential for a complete understanding of the cellular and neurochemical mechanisms underlying physiological control.
the state‐dependent physiology of sleep and wake is not a source of unwanted noise to be eliminated, but rather is a source of important physiological information.
sleep is not a passive state, but an active state of the nervous system.
